canonical_statement: The 2017 document is a selective update of the 2009 KDIGO CKD-MBD guideline for adults and children with CKD, chronic dialysis, or a kidney transplant.
The evidence review searched MEDLINE and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from December 2006 through September 2015, with a one-year overlap from the prior search.
The Work Group supplemented the formal search with articles provided through February 2017.
Across research questions, eligible studies had to report original data in English, follow at least 10 patients with CKD for at least 6 months, and address one of the prespecified research questions.
One evidence-review-team member abstracted data into modified evidence tables and a second reviewer confirmed the abstraction.
Two reviewers independently assessed risk of bias, using the Cochrane tool for randomized trials and the Quality in Prognosis Studies tool for observational studies.
The Work Group used a structured GRADE-based process, evidence profiles, and evidence matrices to grade outcome evidence, overall evidence, and recommendation strength.
The draft guideline underwent open public review, and the Work Group reviewed and considered submitted feedback before finalization.
The systematic review process retrieved 13,530 records, reviewed 11,686 abstracts and 1,519 full texts, and included 117 studies reported in 128 articles.

The September 2017 correction changed the comparator named in Supplemental Table 21 for two Di Iorio studies from calcium acetate to calcium carbonate; the Work Group stated that its conclusions were unchanged.
For adults with CKD, monitor serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and alkaline phosphatase activity beginning in CKD G3a.
For children with CKD, begin monitoring serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and alkaline phosphatase activity in CKD G2.
In CKD G3a-G5D, base monitoring frequency for calcium, phosphate, and PTH on the presence and magnitude of abnormalities and the rate of CKD progression.
In CKD G3a-G3b, a reasonable interval is every 6-12 months for calcium and phosphate; PTH frequency should depend on the baseline level and CKD progression.
In CKD G4, a reasonable interval is every 3-6 months for calcium and phosphate and every 6-12 months for PTH.
In CKD G5, including G5D, a reasonable interval is every 1-3 months for calcium and phosphate and every 3-6 months for PTH.
In CKD G4-G5D, alkaline phosphatase activity may reasonably be measured every 12 months, or more often when PTH is elevated.
Increase measurement frequency when CKD-MBD treatment is being given or biochemical abnormalities are present, to follow trends, efficacy, and adverse effects.
In CKD G3a-G5D, 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels may be measured, with repeat testing determined by baseline values and therapeutic interventions.
Correct vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency in CKD G3a-G5D using treatment strategies recommended for the general population.
Base therapeutic decisions in CKD G3a-G5D on trends rather than a single laboratory value, considering all available CKD-MBD assessments.
Use serum calcium and phosphate values together to guide practice rather than the mathematical calcium-phosphate product.
Clinical laboratories reporting CKD-MBD tests should identify the assay method and report changes in methods, sample source, or handling specifications.
In CKD G3a-G5D with CKD-MBD and/or osteoporosis risk factors, use BMD testing to assess fracture risk when the result will affect treatment decisions.
In CKD G3a-G5D, consider bone biopsy when knowing the type of renal osteodystrophy would affect treatment decisions.
In CKD G3a-G5D, serum PTH or bone-specific alkaline phosphatase can be used to evaluate bone disease because markedly high or low values predict underlying bone turnover.
Do not routinely measure bone-derived collagen synthesis and breakdown markers in CKD G3a-G5D.
Measure length at least quarterly in infants with CKD G2-G5D and assess linear growth at least annually in children with CKD G2-G5D.
In CKD G3a-G5D, lateral abdominal radiography may be used to detect vascular calcification and echocardiography to detect valvular calcification as reasonable alternatives to CT-based imaging.
Consider patients with CKD G3a-G5D and known vascular or valvular calcification to be at highest cardiovascular risk.
It is reasonable to use known vascular or valvular calcification to guide CKD-MBD management.
Base CKD-MBD treatment in CKD G3a-G5D on serial assessments of phosphate, calcium, and PTH considered together.
In CKD G3a-G5D, lower elevated phosphate levels toward the normal range.
In adults with CKD G3a-G5D, avoid hypercalcemia.
In children with CKD G3a-G5D, maintain serum calcium in the age-appropriate normal range.
In CKD G5D, use a dialysate calcium concentration between 1.25 and 1.50 mmol/L, equivalent to 2.5 to 3.0 mEq/L.
Base decisions about phosphate-lowering treatment on progressively or persistently elevated serum phosphate.
In adults with CKD G3a-G5D receiving phosphate-lowering treatment, restrict the dose of calcium-based phosphate binders.
In children with CKD G3a-G5D, it is reasonable to base the choice of phosphate-lowering treatment on serum calcium levels.
Avoid long-term use of aluminum-containing phosphate binders in CKD G3a-G5D.
In CKD G5D, avoid dialysate aluminum contamination to prevent aluminum intoxication.
Limit dietary phosphate intake when treating hyperphosphatemia, either alone or with other treatments.
When making dietary phosphate recommendations, it is reasonable to consider phosphate source, including animal, vegetable, and additive sources.
In CKD G5D with persistent hyperphosphatemia, increase dialytic phosphate removal.
In CKD G3a-G5 not on dialysis, the optimal PTH level is unknown.

When intact PTH is progressively rising or persistently above the assay upper limit in CKD G3a-G5 not on dialysis, evaluate modifiable factors including hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, high phosphate intake, and vitamin D deficiency.
In adults with CKD G3a-G5 not on dialysis, do not routinely use calcitriol or vitamin D analogs.
It is reasonable to reserve calcitriol or vitamin D analogs for CKD G4-G5 with severe and progressive hyperparathyroidism.
In children, calcitriol or vitamin D analogs may be considered to maintain serum calcium in the age-appropriate normal range.
In CKD G5D, maintain iPTH at approximately 2 to 9 times the assay upper normal limit.
Marked PTH changes in either direction within the approximately 2-to-9-times range should prompt initiation or modification of therapy to avoid progression outside the range.
For CKD G5D requiring PTH-lowering therapy, use calcimimetics, calcitriol, vitamin D analogs, or a combination of calcimimetics with calcitriol or a vitamin D analog.
For CKD G3a-G5D with severe hyperparathyroidism that fails medical or pharmacologic therapy, perform parathyroidectomy.
Treat CKD G1-G2 patients with osteoporosis and/or high fracture risk according to general-population management.
In CKD G3a-G3b with normal PTH and osteoporosis and/or high fracture risk, treat as for the general population.

In CKD G3a-G5D with biochemical CKD-MBD abnormalities plus low BMD and/or fragility fractures, treatment choices should account for the magnitude and reversibility of biochemical abnormalities and CKD progression, with consideration of bone biopsy.

In children and adolescents with CKD G2-G5D and CKD-related height deficits, use recombinant human growth hormone when additional growth is desired after first addressing malnutrition and biochemical CKD-MBD abnormalities.
In the immediate post-kidney-transplant period, measure serum calcium and phosphate at least weekly until stable.
After the immediate post-transplant period, base calcium, phosphate, and PTH monitoring frequency on the presence and magnitude of abnormalities and the rate of CKD progression.
In CKD G1T-G3bT, a reasonable interval is every 6-12 months for calcium and phosphate, with PTH measured once and repeated according to baseline level and CKD progression.
In CKD G4T, a reasonable interval is every 3-6 months for calcium and phosphate and every 6-12 months for PTH.
In CKD G5T, a reasonable interval is every 1-3 months for calcium and phosphate and every 3-6 months for PTH.
In CKD G3aT-G5T, alkaline phosphatase may reasonably be measured annually, or more often when PTH is elevated.
Increase monitoring frequency after transplant when CKD-MBD treatment is being given or biochemical abnormalities are present.
It is reasonable to manage post-transplant CKD-MBD biochemical abnormalities as for CKD G3a-G5.
In CKD G1T-G5T, 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels may be measured, with repeat testing determined by baseline values and interventions.
In CKD G1T-G5T, correct vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency using treatment strategies recommended for the general population.
In CKD G1T-G5T with osteoporosis risk factors, use BMD testing to assess fracture risk if results will alter therapy.
During the first 12 months after kidney transplant, when eGFR is greater than about 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and BMD is low, consider vitamin D, calcitriol/alfacalcidol, and/or antiresorptive therapy.
Post-transplant bone-treatment choices should be influenced by CKD-MBD abnormalities in calcium, phosphate, PTH, alkaline phosphatases, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
It is reasonable to consider bone biopsy to guide treatment in the first 12 months after kidney transplant when eGFR is greater than about 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and BMD is low.
The guideline states that data are insufficient to guide treatment of low BMD after the first 12 months following kidney transplant.
In CKD G4T-G5T with known low BMD, manage as for CKD G4-G5 not on dialysis, as detailed in Chapters 4.1 and 4.2.
The guideline reports that four prospective adult cohort studies consistently found lower DXA BMD to predict incident fractures across CKD G3a-G5D.
In the guideline-reported hemodialysis cohort of 485 patients, each standard-deviation higher femoral-neck BMD was associated with a fracture hazard ratio of 0.65 (95% CI 0.47-0.90).
In the guideline-reported Health ABC analysis, the fracture hazard ratio for each standard-deviation lower femoral-neck BMD was 2.69 (95% CI 1.96-3.69) among participants with CKD.
In the same guideline-reported analysis, the adjusted hip-fracture hazard ratio per standard-deviation lower femoral-neck BMD was 5.82 (95% CI 3.27-10.35) among participants with CKD.
In the guideline-reported West cohort, each standard-deviation lower total-hip BMD was associated with an adjusted fracture odds ratio of 1.75 (95% CI 1.30-2.20).
The guideline reports that FRAX with or without BMD and femoral-neck T-score predicted major osteoporotic fracture in the Naylor cohort, with AUCs approximately 0.65-0.71.
In a guideline-reported cohort of 171 children with CKD G2-G5D, the fracture hazard ratio was 1.75 (95% CI 1.15-2.67) per unit lower cortical BMD Z-score.

The guideline reports a post hoc denosumab analysis showing fracture-risk reduction and BMD improvement in 2,817 women with CKD G3a-G3b and 73 with CKD G4; it also flags hypocalcemia risk in advanced CKD.

A KDIGO-led diagnostic study of 492 dialysis patients found iPTH, whole PTH, and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase associated with bone turnover, but no marker alone or in combination was sufficiently robust to classify low, normal, and high turnover in an individual patient.

The Work Group removed the prior requirement for bone biopsy before antiresorptive therapy because experience with osteoporosis drugs in CKD had grown, fracture risk is high, and CKD studies had not definitively shown that bisphosphonates cause adynamic bone disease.
The guideline notes a major lack of fracture-prevention trial data for osteoporosis medications in advanced CKD, especially CKD G5-G5D.

The Work Group concluded that treatment should focus on overt hyperphosphatemia rather than maintaining normal phosphate proactively in CKD G3a-G4 because efficacy and safety data for preventive phosphate lowering were inadequate.
The guideline states that trial data showing phosphate-lowering treatment improves patient-centered outcomes were lacking.

The guideline reports that in a predialysis CKD G3b-G4 placebo-controlled phosphate-binder trial with mean baseline phosphate 4.2 mg/dL, active binder therapy produced only a minimal phosphate decline, did not lower FGF23, and increased coronary calcification scores.

The Work Group considered modest PTH increases a possible adaptive response to declining kidney function and therefore emphasized progressively rising or persistently elevated PTH rather than treating a single value above the assay upper limit.
The guideline reports that recent randomized trials of vitamin D analogs in nondialysis CKD did not improve clinically relevant outcomes and increased hypercalcemia risk.

The guideline notes that EVOLVE did not meet its primary endpoint; subsequent prespecified and post hoc analyses led the Work Group not to exclude possible calcimimetic benefit, but it did not prioritize one PTH-lowering drug class as first-line therapy in CKD G5D.
In kidney transplant recipients, the guideline reports that a denosumab trial improved BMD but observed an increased rate of urinary tract infections.
Supplemental Table 6 rates bisphosphonate effects on BMD as moderate-quality evidence across 6 RCTs (N=1,106) and concludes BMD may improve but results differ by skeletal site.
Supplemental Table 6 rates fracture evidence for bisphosphonates as low quality across 6 RCTs (N=1,106) and reports no difference in fracture incidence.
Supplemental Table 12 includes 5 observational studies (N=3,860), rates fracture-prediction evidence as low quality, and reports a tendency for BMD scores to predict fracture risk.
Supplemental Table 18 includes 2 RCTs (N=485) of dialysate calcium concentrations, rates mortality evidence as very low quality, and reports no mortality effect.
Supplemental Table 24 includes 5 RCTs (N=4,608), rates mortality evidence as moderate quality, and reports possibly lower mortality with non-calcium-containing phosphate binders.
Supplemental Table 24 rates cardiovascular and cerebrovascular event evidence for calcium-containing versus calcium-free phosphate binders as low quality and inconsistent across 3 RCTs (N=3,010).

Supplemental Table 30 contains no eligible mortality, cardiovascular/cerebrovascular, or vascular/valvular calcification outcomes for dietary phosphate interventions and labels these outcome evidence rows very low quality.
Supplemental Table 36 rates mortality evidence for phosphate-binding agents used in high-PTH nondialysis CKD as low quality from one small RCT (N=109) and states that no conclusion can be drawn.
Supplemental Table 42 reports no difference in left-ventricular mass index with vitamin D versus placebo across 2 RCTs (N=222), with moderate-quality evidence.

Supplemental Table 42 rates mortality evidence for vitamin D versus placebo as low quality across 5 RCTs (N=673) and reports no difference in short-term mortality, with few events and mostly one year or less of follow-up.
Supplemental Table 48 rates cinacalcet-versus-placebo mortality evidence as low quality across 4 RCTs (N=5,101) and reports no mortality difference, noting mostly short-term studies and few events.

Supplemental Table 48 reports low-quality evidence of cardiovascular/cerebrovascular benefit for cinacalcet versus placebo from one RCT (N=3,883) and some fracture-rate benefit across 2 RCTs (N=3,965).

Supplemental Table 55 includes 21 observational studies (N=410,950), rates mortality evidence for serum phosphate as low quality, and reports that most studies show increasing death risk with increasing phosphate.

Supplemental Table 55 includes 20 observational studies (N=266,748), rates mortality evidence for serum calcium as low quality, and reports that most studies show increasing death risk with increasing calcium.
Supplemental Table 55 rates evidence linking serum phosphate to GFR decline and cardiovascular/cerebrovascular events as very low quality and inconclusive.
The update addressed selected recommendations rather than re-reviewing every 2009 CKD-MBD recommendation, and the foreword states that substantial evidence gaps remained.
The evidence review generally required at least 6 months of follow-up and used question-specific minimum sample sizes, which excluded shorter or smaller studies by design.
For many interventions and tests, the methodological section states there was no high-quality evidence of net benefit for patient-centered outcomes.
